R01:
*If you have been here before,* the steel doors are open, the lift is waiting with its gate pulled back, and it knows the way. Go straight to the last line.

The steel doors at the end of the Main Corridor have no handle on this side either. They part when you reach them and close behind you without a sound.

Beyond them is a service lift, the old sort, with a brass concertina gate and a panel of round buttons worn hollow by thumbs. There is a button for every floor of St Bede's. All of them are below you.

You drag the gate across. The lift goes down.

It passes G. It passes the Basement, where a stripe of strip-light climbs the gate and is gone. It passes a landing with no number, where somebody out of sight is whistling 'Bright Eyes'. Then it slows, and settles, and stops at a floor that isn't on the panel.

A painted sign on the wall facing the gate, the sort with a pointing hand: WARD 0. RECOVERY. Under it, smaller, in the same council green, somebody has added the year it was last decorated. 1979.

The year Mum did her first night shift here. She was twenty-four. She told you once that she was so frightened that first night she ate a whole packet of custard creams in the sluice, and was sick, and was put on bedpans for a week for wasting biscuits.

The corridor beyond the gate smells of floor polish and pink Hibitane. It runs a long way, under tubes that hum.

*If you have the codeword WARDED,* somewhere down here, a long way off, a mobile phone is ringing. It's Ros's ringtone, the one the phone came with, which she has never bothered to change. It rings out, and starts again.

Turn to {R02}.
R02:
The corridor to Ward 0 is lined with beds on both sides, and every bed is taken.

The Kept, from every decade the hospital has had. A man in striped winceyette with a short back and sides. A girl with crimped hair and a plaster cast covered in felt-tip names. A woman with a Walkman, the foam on her headphones gone to crumbs. They sit up against their pillows, smiling.

As you pass the first bed they all hold out their left wrists together, palm up. Two fingers of each right hand go to the pulse. Their lips move. They are counting, all of them, the same count, in time.

Between the beds stand porters' trolleys, parked nose to tail. Each one is made up: sheet folded back, pillow plumped, a blank card slotted into the holder at the foot. Nobody is with them. As you go by, the nearest one rolls half a turn of its wheels after you, and stops.

Halfway along, the lights go to night setting. The tubes overhead clunk down to a dim amber, one bank at a time, from the far doors towards you.

Then, from behind you, close, in your sister's voice: 'Bean. Bean, wait for me.'

Ros stopped calling you Bean years ago. She hasn't said it once tonight. She says your name, the whole of it, the way you'd write it on a form.

*If Ros is with you,* she is at your elbow, where she has been since the lift. Her mouth is shut. She heard it too. She takes a fistful of your sleeve and does not look round.

If three or more fields of your Wristband are filled, the porters have seen your wrist before you've seen them. Turn to {R03}.

Otherwise, choose.

If you keep walking, eyes front, with the VISITOR'S BADGE on your chest, turn to {R05}.

If Ros is with you and you have the codeword HELD, and you walk on with her hand in yours, turn to {R06}.

If you have the TICKET, and you hold Saturday's ticket up as you walk, turn to {R40}.

If you stop, and wait for the voice behind you, turn to {D09}.
R03:
They step out from between two trolleys: a pair of porters in brown coats shiny at the elbows, keys on long chains. Under the peaks of their caps their faces are creased, pleasant, ordinary. They look at your wrist, not your face.

'Here we are,' says the taller one. 'Been looking all over for you. Up you hop.'

The trolley between them is made up with hospital corners and a cellular blanket turned down, and the card in the holder at its foot has been filled in. Your name, as much of it as your Wristband knows.

The shorter one takes your elbow, gently, to help.

*If Ros is with you,* she gets the strap of her bag round the taller one's wrist and hauls, swearing at him in a level voice, one word at a time, as if she were itemising.

Fight them together, as one.

THE PORTERS   NERVE 9   VIGOUR 10

If you win, turn to {R06}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
R05:
You walk. You look at the far doors and at nothing else.

The badge is clipped where anyone can read it: VISITOR, St Bede's, and your name in biro. A Kept woman in a quilted housecoat reaches out from her bed as you pass. Her fingers stop an inch from your sleeve. She reads the badge, and lowers her hand, and goes back to counting.

'Bean.' Nearer. 'Bean, I've got your coat. You'll catch your death.'

It has the catch in it that Ros's voice had when she was fourteen and trying not to cry in front of you. It knows that. It knows everything you know.

You don't turn round. Rule seven: if the lights dim to night setting, keep walking. Your neck aches with not turning. The amber light lies along the lino, and your shadow goes ahead of you, long and thin, towards the doors.

Gain 1 Fear.

*If Ros is with you,* her shadow lies alongside yours. Each time the voice says Bean, her hand tightens on your sleeve, and she keeps her eyes on the doors too.

The far doors come up out of the amber, closer than they were. Turn to {R06}.
R40:
You take Mum's lottery ticket out of your pocket and hold it up in front of you, at chest height, the way you'd show a pass at a barrier.

Saturday's draw. Her numbers in her own biro: her birthday, Dad's, yours, Ros's, the number of their first house, and a 7 crossed through the middle, continental, because of a fortnight in Benidorm in 1984.

The Kept see it. All down the corridor, faces turn aside on their pillows, eyes screwed shut. It's a small date in a small box. It's a day that hasn't happened, and not one of them can look at it.

The trolleys don't roll. The counting goes on to either side of you, ragged now, losing its place. You walk down the middle of the corridor holding up two quid's worth of syndicate hope, and nothing stops you.

Lose 1 Fear.

*If Ros is with you,* she reads the numbers over your shoulder as you go. 'Twenty-three,' she says. 'That's me. She still does me.'

The doors at the end are painted cream. Turn to {R06}.
D09:
You stop. You turn round.

The lights go down the last notch to night setting and stay there. The amber thickens until your hands are only shapes.

'Bean,' says the voice, close enough now that you feel it on your face. 'Got you.'

It's Ros's voice, all of it, the vowels Toronto has flattened, the catch at the back. But it's kind. It's kinder than Ros has been to you in eight years, warm as a bath, and that is how you know, too late, whose it is. Ros stopped calling you Bean a long time ago. The Notice said keep walking.

A hand finds your wrist and settles two fingers on your pulse. Starched cuff. A fob watch ticks against your knuckle, upside down.

'Seventy-two,' she says, pleased. 'Lovely. We'll have you in a bed in no time.'

*If Ros is with you,* the last thing you feel is her fist letting go of your sleeve, or your sleeve leaving her fist. You never find out which.

Somewhere ahead, a trolley rolls out to meet you, and the sheet is turned down.

Fill in 1 more field on your Wristband. Return to {R01} and choose again.
R06:
The doors at the end are double swing doors with porthole windows, and the portholes have been painted over from the inside, cream. Screwed across both doors at eye height is a sign, so that it splits down the middle when they open: WARD 0 - CLOSED.

Rule five. You've kept the rules all night, the ones you could. This is the one you have to break.

You put your palm flat on the crack between the two halves of the sign, and push.

They open. Warm air comes out, and the smell of a ward at night: polish, Hibitane, boiled milk. Behind you, somewhere back in the amber, the Sister cannot follow you through a door you were told never to open.

She doesn't need to.

She is already inside, at the nurses' station halfway down the ward, under an anglepoise lamp, writing. Starched cap. Silver buckle. Fob watch pinned upside down. She doesn't look up.

'Come in, love,' she says. 'Mind the floor. It's just been done.'

*If Ros is with you,* she comes through the doors half a step after you, so that for a moment it's you who broke the rule and her who followed. 'Noted,' she says, under her breath.

If you have the codeword PROMISE, turn to {R06a}.

Otherwise, turn to {R04}.
R06a:
Just inside the doors, where you walked straight past it, there's a bench: the slatted sort, screwed to the wall, for relatives.

A woman is sitting on it in a purple and teal anorak, with a Woolworths carrier bag on her knee. Through the plastic you can see comics: a Roy of the Rovers, a Shoot!, a Beano folded in half. She has a Lion bar in her other hand, unopened, soft from holding.

'They said he'd gone down to theatre,' she says to you. 'They said wait here. So I've been waiting here.'

You think of a boy in football kit on the Old Wing, and a badge that went to whoever was visiting.

'Gary's on the Old Wing,' you say. 'Up the stairs, through the swing doors. He waited for you. He asked me to tell you. He waited.'

She stands up. She holds the carrier bag against her chest with both arms. 'He's all right?'

'He's waiting,' you say. It's the truest thing you've got.

She goes. Not to the lift: to a door beside it that you hadn't seen, a stairwell, and you hear her trainers on the stairs going up, two at a time, for a long way, until you can't.

Lose 2 Fear.

At the station the Sister turns a page. Turn to {R04}.
R04:
The nurses' station is a long desk with a Formica top, an anglepoise, a Kardex in a steel drum and a row of clipboards on hooks. Glass thermometers stand in a jar of pink solution.

The Sister has gone down the ward. You can hear her somewhere past the curtains, unhurried, the soft tread of her shoes. She has left the night report open on the desk, turned round so it faces you.

*WARD 0. NIGHT REPORT. 22nd/23rd March 1979.*

*Bed 4. Mr A. Kerr, 81. Did not settle. Asked for Sister 02.10, Sister busy. Asked me again 02.40, said he was tired now and would I let him go. I sat with him and held his hand and told him he could. Peaceful. Died 03.15. Last offices done with Staff Nurse. Relatives informed.*

*M. Brennan, Nursing Auxiliary.*

Beside the signature, small, a smiling face with two dots for eyes.

Under it, in a different hand, the upright fountain-pen hand with a hook on every numeral, underlined twice:

*Auxiliary removed rule 8 from the Notice. Not to be replaced.*

You know the round hand. It's on every birthday card in your drawer, on the notes on the fridge telling you what's in the freezer. It's Mum's hand at twenty-four, before the stroke made it slope downhill.

She sat with a stranger at three in the morning and let him go, and then she went to the Notice on the linen-cupboard door and tore off the rule that let her, and kept it. She never told you. She told you about the custard creams.

*If Ros is with you,* she reads it over your shoulder. She lifts her phone to photograph it, then lowers the phone without taking the picture and puts one finger on the smiling face instead, the way you'd touch a bruise.

Down the ward, the soft shoes stop, and turn, and start back.

Turn to {R07}.
R07:
The Sister comes back up the ward into the circle of the anglepoise and sits. She takes a buff folder from the rack. It has your name on the front, in her hand.

'Just catching up on your notes, love,' she says. 'Won't keep you.'

She reads them to you. She doesn't need to look down. Everything you were offered tonight, and what you said to it. Every time you gave somebody your name, and who. Every cup of tea, the ones you drank and the ones you let go cold. The fields on your Wristband, in the order they went in, with the times.

Her voice doesn't change for any of it. It's the warmest voice you've heard all night, and it makes you want to own up to things.

When she has finished she closes the folder, lifts her fob watch on its pin and turns it up to read it. She looks at the watch. She looks at you. She is checking one against the other: every round she has done tonight, a tick at a time, in a column you can't see but can feel.

*If Ros is with you,* she has her phone out and is typing with both thumbs. When you look, it's a list of everything the Sister has just said, timed to the minute. She doesn't seem to know she's doing it.

If you have not ticked the 05:00 box of your ROUNDS, turn to {R08}.

If you have ticked the 05:00 box, turn to {R09}.
R08:
The watch goes back on its pin. The Sister opens her mouth to speak.

From the far end of the ward, from behind the last curtain, Bay 6, comes a voice like gravel in a bucket.

'Bean? Is that you making that racket?'

Hoarse from the tube. Cross. Half asleep and entirely herself. It's the voice through the bathroom door on Saturday mornings, telling you to turn that music down. It's Mum.

The Sister's pen stops.

Something on your wrist lets go. You look down. One of the fields on your Wristband, filled in tonight in a hand that wasn't yours, has gone blank: only the printed word and a line. The skin under it is cool.

The voice doesn't come again. The curtain round Bay 6 hangs still. But you heard it, and the Sister heard it, and her pen is still not moving.

Cross off one field of your Wristband. Lose 2 Fear.

*If Ros is with you,* she has gone white. 'That was her,' she says. 'That was actually her. Wasn't it?' You nod. Ros doesn't write anything down.

Turn to {R10}.
R09:
The watch goes back on its pin. The Sister sighs: the small, fond sigh of a nurse whose patient has been out of bed again.

'You're late, love,' she says.

She opens your folder at the back. She uncaps her pen.

She takes your wrist in her cool fingers, turns it over, finds the next empty field on your Wristband and fills it in, neatly, holding your pulse with her other hand while she writes. You watch your own details go in. She doesn't hurry. She makes each letter clear, for the night staff after her.

'There,' she says. 'Now we know where you are.'

Above the station a clock with a red second hand says five o'clock. You didn't notice it get there.

Fill in 1 more field on your Wristband.

*If Ros is with you,* she watches the pen go across your wrist and takes a step towards the desk, and stops, because the Sister has looked up at her, pleasantly, and the look says she's next.

Turn to {R10}.
R10:
The Sister turns back to her notes. The interview, it seems, is over. The anglepoise hums.

You look at your wrist under the lamp. NAME. DATE OF BIRTH. NEXT OF KIN. WARD. BED. Some filled, some not, in her hand, the ink sunk into the plastic.

Fields don't come off because you want them off. You've picked at them with a thumbnail all night and the ink stays where she put it. They come off when somebody claims you back: when somebody who loves you says the true thing out loud, or cuts you loose.

Mum's letter is in your pocket, in its envelope. For Bean.

*If Ros is with you,* she's looking at your wrist too. Her bag is on her shoulder, and her hand is inside it, resting on something.

Past the station, the ward goes on: curtained bays down both sides, six of them, and at the far end the one with its curtain half drawn. Bay 6.

If Ros is with you, and you give her MUM'S LETTER to read aloud, turn to {R11}.

If Ros is with you and you have the codeword HELD, and you hold out your wrist for her scissors, turn to {R12}.

If you go on into the ward, turn to {R13}.
R11:
You hold out the envelope. For Bean, in Mum's hand.

Ros looks at it for a long moment before she takes it. She knew what was in it before you did. She has known for three years.

She unfolds the letter and reads it aloud in her list voice, the one she uses on site meetings and airline helplines: flat, clear, every word given the same weight, so nobody can say afterwards that they misheard.

She gets as far as the comma in the middle, and the word just before it, the one Mum uses on everybody from the bin men to the consultant, and she can't.

She stops. She breathes through her nose. At the station the Sister writes, and doesn't look up.

Ros reads it anyway. Her voice goes, and she carries on without it, in a whisper, to the end, to the last word.

'One,' she says.

Something on your wrist lets go. A field is blank. Ros folds the letter along its old creases and gives it back to you, and doesn't let go of it straight away.

Cross off one field of your Wristband.

Turn to {R13}.
R12:
Ros takes her hand out of her bag. She's holding a pair of surgical scissors, steel, blunt-nosed, the kind for cutting off dressings.

'Don't ask,' she says. 'Hold still.'

You hold still. She slides the lower blade under your Wristband, against the skin, where the plastic sits tight over the bone. The steel is cold. She finds the edge of one filled field and cuts round it in three small snips, the way she'd cut out a coupon, and the last snip catches you.

It stings. It is skin, nearly. A bead of blood comes up on the side of your wrist, and the square of plastic drops on the lino, blank side up.

At the station, the Sister's pen pauses, and goes on.

'There,' says Ros. She puts the scissors away. Her hands are steady until they're back inside the bag.

Cross off one field of your Wristband. Lose 1 Vigour.

Turn to {R13}.
R13:
The first bay past the station has its curtains open and its bed stripped to the mattress, blue-and-white ticking. A card on the rail says BAY 1.

Bay 2's curtain is drawn all the way round.

Behind it, a mobile phone is ringing. A modern phone, the stock ringtone, muffled, the way a phone sounds in a coat pocket. It rings out, and stops, and starts again.

Pinned to the outside of the curtain at eye height is a card with the patient's initial on it. R.

*If Ros is with you,* she puts her hand to her own coat pocket. Her phone is there, and silent. She takes it out and looks at it anyway, at the empty signal bars, and puts it back. 'Everybody has that ringtone,' she says.

Further down, past Bay 2, the ward goes on: four more bays, a clipboard hung at the foot of every bed, and the far curtain half drawn.

If you have the codeword WARDED, and you open the curtain of Bay 2, turn to {R14}.

If you walk on to the charts, turn to {R16}.
R14:
You pull the curtain back along its runners.

Ros is in the bed. She is under a cellular blanket, tucked in tight, her arms on top of it and her hands folded. Her coat is on the chair with her bag, and the phone is ringing in the coat. Her hair has been brushed. Ros has never let anybody brush her hair.

She is smiling, wide and settled, a smile that doesn't fit her face. Her eyes are open on the ceiling tiles, perfectly content.

Her wristband is full. ROSALIND, it says, and her date of birth, and in the box for next of kin, in the Sister's careful hand, your name. Ward 0. Bay 2. Every field.

The phone stops. On the screen, before it dims, you see who has been calling. HOME. Mum's landline, in the house where you live, where nobody is tonight to call anybody.

The clipboard at the foot of the bed holds her obs, hourly since she came in, and every one is the same.

If you have the codeword SPOKE but not MENDED, and you say her name and then keep going and say the rest, it will take long enough to cost you: turn to {R41}.

If you say her name, turn to {R15}.

If you leave her and go on to Mum, turn to {R16}.
R15:
'Ros.'

Nothing. The smile stays.

You say it again: the short one, the one only family uses, the one you've been saying at her in your head for eight years in tones of voice you never used out loud. 'Ros.'

At the station the Sister lifts her head and listens, and frowns down at her page, at a word she can't make out.

Ros blinks. The smile goes out of her face from the edges inwards, and what's left is Ros: crumpled, cross, nobody's patient.

'Did I miss it?' She sits up, and the blanket slides off. 'Did they ring? Did I miss it?'

'No,' you say. 'You haven't missed anything.'

She looks at her wrist. The fields are fading, letter by letter, back to blank. She doesn't ask. She swings her legs out of the bed, pulls her boots on, stands, and holds on to your arm until the floor settles.

Cross off the codeword WARDED. Note the codeword HELD.

Turn to {R16}.
R41:
'Ros,' you say.

She doesn't move. You say it again. Then, because you're here and she's lying down and for once she can't get up and walk off, you keep going.

'She asked me to stay,' you say. 'Mum. After the first stroke. I was sitting on the end of her bed on the stroke unit and she couldn't do her buttons, and she got hold of my sleeve and she said, Stay with me. Don't let them put me anywhere.'

Ros's eyes are still on the ceiling. Her smile is still wrong.

'So I stayed. And I let you think I chose it. I let you think I was the good one and you were the one who went. I liked it. It was the only thing I had that you didn't.'

At the station the Sister has stopped writing. She gets up. She comes down the ward, unhurried, and stands at the foot of the bed. 'Wrist, please, love,' she says, and you give it to her, because you are not going to stop talking to do anything else.

She fills in a field. You keep talking. You tell Ros about the commode, and the night Mum didn't know who you were, and the night you sat in the car on the drive and screamed with the windows up. Six years. It takes a long time.

Ros blinks.

'She sent me,' Ros says. Her voice is thick with sleep, and it's hers. 'After Dad's funeral. In the kitchen, with the sandwiches. She said, Go. Take the job. If you stay, your sister will let you do everything and never have a life.'

She turns her head on the pillow and looks at you.

'So I went. And I let you think I'd left you. It was easier being the one who left than the one who was sent.'

Neither of you says anything for a while. The Sister goes back up the ward to her desk. On Ros's wrist, the fields are going blank, one by one.

'Right,' says Ros. 'Well. That's two of us, then.'

She holds out her hand, and you pull her up out of the bed.

Fill in 1 more field on your Wristband. Cross off the codeword WARDED. Note the codewords HELD and MENDED.

Turn to {R16}.
R16:
*If you have been here before,* the ward is as you left it, the clipboards hung straight, the round somewhere behind the curtains. Go straight to the choices.

You stand at the head of the bays with the station at your back.

Ward 0 runs away from you down both sides. Bay 3, Bay 4, Bay 5: curtains open, a bed in each, a Kept patient in each bed, smiling, and at the foot of every bed a clipboard with an obs chart.

At the far end, Bay 6, its curtain half drawn. Through the gap you can see the end of a bed and two feet under a blanket. You know those feet. You cut those toenails.

You know charts. Six years of district nurses and discharge letters, of writing her blood pressure in a notebook on the kitchen table. You know what a right one looks like. And you know the Sister's hand, because you've watched it all night: blue-black fountain pen, upright, a little hook on every numeral.

Every chart on this ward is in her hand. Every patient is who their chart says. Every entry is timed at or before the hour on the station clock, because she doesn't write down what hasn't happened yet.

The ward keeps the same rule as everywhere else tonight. Read each chart. If nothing is wrong, walk on. If something is wrong, turn back. Get it right all the way down, and the ward will let you reach Bay 6.

*If Ros is with you,* she reads the first chart over your shoulder, frowning, counting under her breath. 'Temperature, pulse, resp, BP,' she says. 'Tell me what normal is. I'll check your working.'

If you have Mum's GLASSES and put them on first, turn to {R17}.

If you begin, turn to {R18}.
R17:
You take Mum's reading glasses out of your pocket. Tortoiseshell, from the optician in the precinct, the left arm held on at the hinge with Sellotape you wound on yourself in August because she wouldn't wait for the optician.

Plus two and a half. They should make everything swim. You put them on.

The numbers come sharp. Every figure on every clipboard as far as Bay 5 stands up off the paper, black and exact, the hooks on the Sister's numerals clear as print. You can see the dots on the temperature graphs. You can see where the nib caught.

They smell of her: Nivea, and the inside of her handbag.

Lose 1 Fear.

*If Ros is with you,* she looks at you in Mum's glasses and laughs, once, out of nowhere, and puts her hand over her mouth. 'Sorry,' she says. 'You look exactly like her.'

Turn to {R18}.
R18:
Bay 3. A man of about sixty in striped winceyette pyjamas buttoned to the throat, his hair Brylcreemed flat. Kept, smiling at you over the turned-down sheet. On his locker, a glass with his teeth in it and a folded Daily Herald.

You lift the clipboard off its hook.

*WARD 0. BED 3. HARGREAVES, Thomas. Admitted 4.11.52.*

A TPR chart, the old kind, a graph on squared paper. Temperature in Fahrenheit, as they did then: 98.4, 98.4, 98.4, the dots joined in a flat blue line. Pulse 72. Respirations 16. Blood pressure 130 over 85.

Every hour from ten at night to the hour on the station clock, every entry in blue-black fountain pen, upright, with a hook on every numeral.

You read it twice: the name, the date, the times. Mr Hargreaves watches you, delighted, as though you were a grandchild who'd come to visit.

You hang the clipboard back on its hook.

If nothing is wrong, and you walk on, turn to {R19}.

If something is wrong, and you turn back, turn to {R22}.
R19:
Bay 4. A woman in a pink quilted bed jacket, her hair set in rollers under a net. Kept, smiling, her hands folded on a Mills & Boon. She smells of Yardley.

The clipboard:

*WARD 0. BED 4. PRICE, Edna. Admitted 21.3.79.*

March 1979. Mum's month. Down the page goes the Sister's fountain pen: temperature 36.9, pulse 80, respirations 18, blood pressure 140 over 90, hourly from ten o'clock, a hook on every numeral.

Except the line for three o'clock.

The three o'clock obs are in a different hand: small square capitals, engineer's capitals, a line struck through every zero. You've seen that hand on eight years of birthday cards from Toronto, on the backs of photographs, on careful lists of what Mum's pension goes on. It's Ros's.

The numbers are right. 36.9. 80. 18. 140 over 90.

Mrs Price turns a page of her book.

If you turn back, and Ros is with you, and you have the codeword MENDED, turn to {R25}.

If you turn back, and you do not have MENDED, or you have the codeword WARDED, turn to {R20}.

If you walk on, turn to {R22}.
R25:
You turn back. The ward turns with you, every curtain swinging on its rail, and when it settles Ros is holding the clipboard.

She has it close to her face, looking at the three o'clock line. 'That's mine,' she says. 'That's my writing. I've never been in here.'

She looks down the ward at Bay 6, at the two feet under the blanket. Then she looks at you, and you watch her decide.

'I'm the one she named,' she says. 'On the form. Me. Let me do this.' She's already working out how, in a list. 'Temperature, pulse, resp, BP, sats. Every hour. Tonight, and whatever comes after tonight. I've watched you do it. I can do it. Let me be the one, for once.'

Her hands are shaking on the clipboard. Six years of her not being here stand between you in the aisle, and so does everything you finally said to each other tonight.

If you let her be the one, turn to {R26}.

If you take the chart off her, because you have done this for six years, turn to {R27}.
R26:
You let her.

It's the hardest thing you've done tonight, and you've done some things. You stand at her elbow with your hands in your pockets and watch your sister take Mum's obs.

Her hands shake. She counts the pulse twice because she lost her place the first time. She writes the numbers in the next column in her square capitals, a slash through every zero, and they're right. All of them. You check. Of course you check.

Every number she writes is one you didn't. Six years of being the only person alive who knew what Mum's blood pressure was on any given Tuesday, and now there are two of you, and one of you lives in Toronto. It was always going to cost something. You didn't know it would cost this.

Gain 2 Fear.

She hangs the clipboard back on its hook, squares it, and looks at you. 'Was that all right?'

'Yeah,' you say. 'That was all right.'

The ward has turned while you weren't looking. Turn to {R20}.
R27:
You hold out your hand for the chart.

'Six years,' you say. 'I've done her obs for six years, Ros. I know her numbers. I know what her BP does after a curry. I know which arm. You don't get to fly in at the end and—'

You stop, because she has already let go.

She puts the clipboard into your hand carefully, the way you'd pass somebody a hot plate. She lets go of it, and you watch her let go of something else as well, behind her face: something she was holding out to you a moment ago.

'Right,' she says. 'Of course.'

She steps back. She folds her arms. She looks at Bay 6 and not at you. You hang the clipboard on its hook and nobody says anything, and it's easier, it's so much easier, and you're ashamed of how much easier it is.

Cross off the codeword MENDED. Lose 1 Fear.

R20:

You get good at it. You were always good at it. You learn to walk so that your shoes make no sound. You learn the voice: warm, unhurried, never surprised. You learn that the kindest thing is to take a pulse and keep it.

Tonight it's a man in a work fleece and a woman in a good coat who has just flown in from somewhere, sitting at opposite ends of the room, not speaking. You know them. You've never met them. You know them.

You stand in the doorway with your torch, red filter, and your watch upside down.

'Can I get you two a cup of tea?' you say. 'You look done in.'
E_ADMITTED:
Wherever you are, the round finds you.

It doesn't hurry. It doesn't need to. Your Wristband is full, or the last hour has come round, or you're simply too frightened to stand up any more, and on a ward at night it all comes to the same thing. You have stopped being a visitor.

Soft shoes. A red torch, coming bed by bed. A fob watch, upside down.

'Here we are, love,' she says.

Your bed is made up. You don't remember it being there, but in a hospital at night a bed always is. Clean sheets, a cellular blanket, one pillow and a spare. A card at the foot with your name on it, all of it, in her upright hand.

She helps you in. She takes your shoes off for you and stands them side by side under the bed. She tucks the blanket in on both sides, firm, hospital corners, so that you're held. She takes your pulse with two fingers and writes it down, and smiles.

'Seventy-two,' she says. 'Perfect.'

*If Ros is with you,* Ros is at the foot of the bed, saying your name. Then the Sister draws the curtain round on its rail, and Ros is a shape on the other side of it, and then a shape walking away, and then a phone ringing somewhere a long way off that nobody answers.

The lights go to night setting. Bank by bank the tubes clunk down to amber, ward by ward, all through St Bede's, until yours goes too. You know the rule. If the lights dim, keep walking. You're in bed. You're tucked in. You can't.

Down the ward, in a bed like yours, somebody is smiling at the ceiling. You find that you are smiling too. You can feel it, wide and settled, a smile for a photograph. You have never been so frightened, and the smile doesn't move.

It's so nice to be looked after. You haven't been, in years.

Every hour, all night, which is for ever, somebody comes to see how you are.
E_ONLYCHILD:
At six o'clock the ward is a recovery ward, and you're standing in it on your own.

They bring Mum through from theatre under a foil blanket, small and grey and wired to everything, and she lives. That's the first thing, and it's the thing you will say to people afterwards, because it's true. She lives.

Later, when the tube is out, she opens her eyes and finds you at the end of the bed, and looks past you, and says, 'Where's your sister?'

'Toronto,' you say. You don't know why.

Mum nods, as if that's where Ros always is.

You go up to Level 3 to get your coat. Ros's wheelie case is in the family room, by the plastic chairs, with the airline tag still on the handle. You take it with you. Nobody stops you.

Out in the car park the fog is lifting in strips. You stand by the Corsa and ring her. Her phone rings. Somewhere inside St Bede's, through the concrete, a long way down, you can hear it: the stock ringtone, the one she never changed, on the Old Wing or under it. It rings out. You ring again.

Nobody else asks about her. Her office in Toronto sends one email, and then doesn't. Her flat is let to somebody else. When you say her name to people they nod politely, and change the subject, and don't remember afterwards that you said it.

Mum comes home in December. You do her obs. You do her tablets, her dosette box, her hoist, her forms, her phone calls. You're good at it. You do it by yourself.

Every night at twenty to two, you ring Ros's number from the kitchen, and you hold the phone away from your ear, and listen. Across town, under the hospital, faint, a phone is ringing in a coat on a chair.

It rings out, and starts again.
E_LOOP:
The tone goes on, and on, and then it's the hum of a vending machine, a note too low.

You're sitting on a plastic chair in the family room on Level 3. Box of tissues. A kettle with no water in it. A poster about stroke: Face, Arms, Speech, Time. Mum's property bag on the chair beside you, zipped. The clock over the door says 01:40.

You know this. You know the hand-gel dispenser that clicks out in the corridor when nobody passes it.

You know the lights are going to go down to night setting, bank by bank. You know the shoes that never hurry, and the tea, and what the tea costs. You know it the way you know a dream on the second time through, and the knowing is going, already, draining out of the back of your head.

What stays is one thing. There's a sentence you've carried for eight years, the one you said at the funeral, and another under it you've never said at all.

Footsteps in the corridor, quick ones, and the rattle of a wheelie case.

The door opens. Ros comes through it with her phone already out, already opening her mouth.

This time, say it first.
